lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
Date of birth: 14 Nov 1995 | Nationality: Mexican
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Reduced freight costs by 15% by consolidating supplier pickups into regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.

- Scoring 40 vendors weekly on on-time delivery, fill rate, lead-time variance and invoice accuracy, and sharing the scorecards with buyers before each quarterly review, raised on-time inbound deliveries from 81% to 93%.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Cut average order lead time through the warehouse from 10 days to 5 while holding daily throughput constant and doubling work-in-process to keep pickers busy.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Redesigned the pick paths for the fast-moving zone, cutting walking distance per order by 28% and raising picks per labor hour from 92 to 110.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; the findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.
- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations, raising inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5% within a year.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Spearheaded a data-driven, optimization-first transformation of last-mile logistics that unlocked significant efficiency gains.
- Cut average route length from 120 to 90 miles, a 40% reduction, by solving the routing problem with customer time windows.
- Shared the model and a one-page summary with the grocer's dispatch team, who piloted the routes on two trucks for a month.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- Mapped the donation intake process with the warehouse lead and removed two duplicate data-entry steps, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Wrote a slotting guide that the volunteer coordinators used to re-slot the warehouse again after its spring expansion.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python, SAP
Methods: demand forcasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: Date of birth and nationality should be removed from the résumé.
items.because: Readers should not weigh them when assessing qualifications, and they can distract from relevant experience and education.

items.says: Experience appears after Education despite being the strongest evidence of the candidate’s current direction.
items.because: Readers encounter the degree before the more recent, relevant professional experience.

items.says: The reorder-point bullet gives no outcome showing what changed.
items.because: Without a result and comparison, the value of setting the reorder points is hard to judge.

items.says: The bullet does not say who reviewed the reorder points.
The vendor-scoring process delays the on-time delivery result.
OEE cannot be 112% under the conventional definition.
items.because: Availability, performance, and quality are each bounded at 100%, so their product cannot exceed 100%.

items.says: The bullet names areas addressed but not the specific change made.
The lead-time, throughput, and work-in-process claims conflict with Little’s Law.
items.because: At constant throughput, doubling work-in-process implies lead time rising from 10 to 20 days, not falling from 10 to 5.

items.says: The work-in-process increase is presented without explaining its significance.
items.because: Readers may wonder whether it was temporary or affected inventory or service.

items.says: The lengthy throughput and work-in-process explanation weakens the lead-time result.
items.because: It draws attention away from the shorter lead time and introduces an unresolved tradeoff.

items.says: The Crestway bullets cover several operations areas without making their relationship clear.
items.because: The breadth can make the role feel like unrelated tasks rather than a focused supply-chain story.

items.says: The pick-path redesign does not say what guided the layout change.
The time-study wording obscures the candidate’s role in putting the triage station in place.
items.because: “The findings led to” makes the change sound as though it happened on its own.

items.says: The dock-scheduling bullet does not show what rule or constraint shaped the approach.
The opening bullet uses abstract language instead of naming the work and its result.
items.because: Its claims cannot be assessed, despite a route-length result appearing in the next bullet.

items.says: The stated 40% reduction is mathematically wrong; 120 to 90 miles is a 25% reduction.
items.because: The decrease is 30 miles, which is 25% of the original 120 miles.

items.says: The project’s strongest result does not open the entry.
items.because: The route-length result is more concrete than the opening bullet’s broad transformation claim.

items.says: The route-length comparison lacks the number of routes or the period measured.
The routing bullet names the time-window constraint but not how the problem was solved.
The method follows the metric without adding another result; put the result first for scanability.
The pilot’s scope is given, but its result is not.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether dispatch or route outcomes improved.

items.says: The recommendations bullet does not say whether leadership adopted the advice or what resulted.
items.because: Without an outcome or evidence of implementation, the value of the advice is hard to assess.

items.says: “Analyzed warehouse operations” does not identify the analysis used.
The donation-intake bullet would be a stronger opening than the project’s current first bullet.
items.because: It gives a concrete process change and clear result rather than only saying recommendations were made.

items.says: The donation-intake result comes after the process details, slowing the payoff.
The slotting guide’s use is clear, but its operational result is not.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether it improved storage, retrieval, or another warehouse outcome.

items.says: The slotting guide does not say what information or principle informed its recommendations.
“Re-slot the warehouse again” is redundant and leaves the guide’s purpose unclear.
“Forcasting” is misspelled in Skills > Methods.
items.because: The error is visible in a skills label and obscures the intended term.
